item.title: Neuronal communication subspaces arise across prefrontal-striatal circuits prior to gaze-directed object selection and develop with learning
item.description:
Relevance: 36% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Poggi, P. G., Hassani, S.-A., Neumann, A., Brust, D., Boroujeni, K. B., Tiesinga, P., Womelsdorf, T.
How neuronal ensembles determine the most relevant object to attend to remains unresolved but likely involves coordinating information across multiple brain areas. We found support for this hypothesis in latent firing co-variations across the prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and head of the caudate (CD) during and after attention-set learning. Before gaze shifted to an object, neuronal communication subspaces emerged across area pairs. While exploring options during learning, ACC and PFC led communication over the CD prior to gaze shifts, which switched to the CD and PFC leading the ACC when exploiting learned attention sets. Neurons participating in exploration- and exploitation-specific subspaces were partly segregated and carried information about the value and location of the to-be-selected objects, suggesting they guide attention and gaze.

item.title: Sampling the Training Trajectory of Vision Models Reveals a Mismatch with Human Visual Development
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Proietti, M., Bersch, D., Schaumlöffel, T., Cerdas, D. G., Franaszek-Traczewska, A., Zwad, H. E., Xie, S., Baldauf, M., Sylvester, T., Schätz, C. M., Höhl, S., Köster, M., Cichy, R. M., Roig, G.
We compare time-resolved EEG representational geometry across seven age groups, from 6 months to adulthood, with representations sampled throughout training from supervised and self-supervised ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16. Previous model-brain comparisons mostly used adult brain recordings and untrained or fully trained networks. We find that successive training stages do not systematically progress from child- to adult-like neural representations: alignment with every age group from 4 years onward emerges early in training and remains stable. Training adds substantial alignment beyond the untrained architecture, similarly at every age. Finally, categorical structure and spatial frequency each explain a stable share of the neural geometry at every age, with apparent age-related increases in categorical organization reflecting increased EEG reliability. Because standard training on full-resolution images aligns with all ages early, and spatial frequency, which depends on maturing visual acuity, strongly shapes the neural geometry, developmentally structured visual input may help models follow human visual development.

item.title: The Self-Assembling Brain: Emergent Routing and Its Open Challenges
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Dongsung Huh
arXiv:2611.31629v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biologically inspired alternatives to backpropagation, such as feedback alignment, relax the requirement for exact synaptic weight symmetry but still presuppose a fixed, pre-wired correspondence between forward and feedback pathways, an impasse Liao et al. (PNAS, 2026) term "architectural circularity." This commentary examines their Self-Assembling Motif (SAM), which reframes credit assignment as a self-organizing process driven by local synaptic rules. By linking ascending inference and descending feedback streams through initially random cross-stream connections, SAM supports local bridge alignment and emergent pathway alignment during stable training without fixed neuron-to-neuron pairing. Its resulting learning dynamics also exhibit adaptive preconditioning. The commentary highlights the algorithmic, biophysical, and temporal challenges that define the next research frontier: loss of neuron-specific nonlinear gating under straight-through approximation, compounding routing errors in deeper hierarchies, low-dimensional routing bottlenecks, the cortical implementation of non-driving modulatory connections, and the shift from alternating inference-update phases to continuous sensory processing.

item.title: How Experience Becomes a Program: Episodic Memory as a Difference Engine
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
He, Y., Wu, S.
A child who has seen a few sums can add numbers of any length: finite experience has become a program, a procedure with memory that holds for inputs of every size. Networks learn procedures by passing errors backward through every step of a computation, over many examples, and what they learn on short inputs seldom holds on long ones. Brains keep something networks discard, the experiences themselves, and we propose that they keep them in order to compare them. When two remembered experiences differ in one place, the first answer at which they differ depended on that place. This method of difference finds the cause of an answer in one step, however long the computation in between, and finds causes that act jointly, each of which alone is invisible to statistics. We show that such comparisons write programs. Comparing an experience with one that differs in a single symbol shows what each answer depends on; in a memory that recalls the past by counting events, each dependence is a linear equation, and the stack, the queue and the counter of computer science are solutions of such equations. Comparing what follows two beginnings shows which states a program must keep, and comparing a question with the question one symbol shorter builds each answer from the one before. Where experience does not decide, nothing is guessed: the learner asks, or says that it does not know. A machine built on these principles, with no backpropagation and no search over programs, writes exact programs for thirteen of the fifteen tasks of a standard benchmark, each in under a minute, from a few hundred short strings and, for two of the tasks, questions of its own; eleven of the programs hold at a million symbols. It learns tasks withheld from its design, builds multiplication from its own addition, and in 5,680 runs announces no false program. The hippocampus has the form of such a difference engine: it stores whole episodes after one exposure, keeps similar ones apart, recalls a neighbour of the present and compares the two. In simulated circuits of neurons the programs run exactly, a replayed sweep finds where two episodes differ, and a local rule learns the gains with no backward pass. On this account, episodic memory is the brain's means of assigning credit by comparison.

item.title: Subliminal Learning Crosses Modalities
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Saraswathy Amjith, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba, Yoon Kim
arXiv:2611.31870v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.

item.title: Compressible Representations: Functional Spines in Deep Neural Networks
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv AI
Niranjan Rajesh, Meenakshi Khosla
arXiv:2611.31817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.

item.title: The Dead Salmons of AI Interpretability
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv AI
Maxime M\'eloux, Giada Dirupo, Fran\c{c}ois Portet, Maxime Peyrard
arXiv:2512.18792v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In a striking neuroscience study, the authors placed a dead salmon in an MRI scanner and showed it images of humans in social situations. Astonishingly, standard analyses of the time reported brain regions predictive of social emotions. The explanation, of course, was not supernatural cognition but a cautionary tale about misapplied statistical inference. In AI interpretability, reports of similar "dead salmon" artifacts abound: feature attribution, probing, sparse auto-encoding, and even causal analyses can produce plausible-looking explanations for randomly initialized neural networks. Upon inspection of this phenomenon our position is to argue for a pragmatic statistical-causal reframing: explanations of computational systems should be treated as parameters of a (statistical) model, inferred from computational traces. This perspective goes beyond simply measuring statistical variability of explanations due to finite sampling of input data; interpretability methods become statistical estimators, and findings should be tested against explicit and meaningful alternative computational hypotheses, with uncertainty quantified with respect to the postulated statistical model. It also highlights important theoretical issues, such as the identifiability of common interpretability queries, which we argue is critical to understand the field's susceptibility to false discoveries, poor generalizability, and high variance.

item.title: Normative and neural network models of multisensory integration
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Marcus Ghosh, John S. Butler
arXiv:2611.32829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Animals continuously detect scents, sights and sounds, which their brains combine into diverse multisensory streams. Multisensory integration accelerates learning, increases reaction speeds and helps to resolve sensory ambiguities. In studying this process, the field has developed a continuum of models; from concise mathematical equations, with a handful of variables, to artificial neural networks, with billions of parameters. In this review, we divide this spectrum into two classes: normative models start from a hypothesis about how multisensory signals should be integrated, while neural network models aim to emulate how circuits could integrate them. Together, these models demonstrate that observers can integrate cues in a statistically optimal fashion, and help to explain experimental findings, including the diversity of multisensory neuron response profiles and network architectures. In this review, we provide a didactic overview of multisensory models, complete with accessible equations and Python code, and compare their assumptions and explanatory power. We detail what has been learned from these models. Finally, we discuss how the ideas and insights from classical theoretical models can be reconciled with those from artificial neural networks, and how this convergence should shape future research.

item.title: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Patricio M. Vera
arXiv:2611.14116v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? We studied word extension across ten visual representations: eight trained encoders, a randomly initialized network, and raw pixels. Reanalyzing trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018; 520 people), we computed each test image's distance to the teaching examples. Within the taught domain, greater distance was associated with less extension for all eight trained encoders and for the untrained network, so the association cannot be attributed only to what the encoders learned; raw pixels showed no negative association. In post hoc models that let the distance slope vary across images, seven of the eight trained encoders retained a negative estimate and five had 95% intervals entirely below zero; the interval of the reference encoder included zero. Whether trial order changes the distance slope, the frozen primary question, remained inconclusive. Example composition changed extension at comparable distances: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. In artificial learners, words joining more distant categories were learned less accurately for six of the eight trained encoders. Every trained encoder correlated with human similarity measures from three datasets, and so did the untrained network, although far more weakly than the trained encoders other than MAE on two of them. In an exploratory comparison on the same images, no common threshold on any trained encoder reproduced the adults' narrow-to-broad gain (at most 66.67 vs. 76.43 percentage points). Cosine distance to the centroid of the teaching examples predicts part of word extension, but does not capture the effect of example composition.

item.title: Eliciting sandbagged LLM capability via structural interventions on attention-head functional networks
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Manzi Fabrice Niyigaba, Ishan Verma Prasad, Sansheng Cao, Zheng Huang, Yujun Yan
arXiv:2611.31615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliably evaluating the capabilities of advanced AI systems is critical for safe development and deployment, yet such evaluations may be undermined by sandbagging, a situation in which a model strategically suppresses capabilities it possesses. Existing work has developed controlled sandbagging settings and methods for detecting or eliciting hidden capabilities, but comparatively little is known about how a model's internal neural computation changes when its capabilities are suppressed. In this work, we study sandbagging through the lens of internal functional organization. Inspired by network neuroscience, we construct functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions while holding the model architecture and weights fixed. Surprisingly, across model architectures and community detection methods, we find a consistent structural signature in which sandbagging is associated with reduced functional connectivity within detected communities. We further demonstrate that this reorganization can guide capability elicitation. Ablating attention heads that exhibit the largest connectivity changes substantially recovers suppressed performance while largely preserving performance under honest behavior. Moreover, incorporating these structural signals further improves existing inference-level and weight-level elicitation methods. Together, our results show that sandbagging is accompanied by systematic reorganization of internal computation and demonstrate that functional network structure can provide both a mechanistic lens for understanding capability suppression and a practical signal for recovering hidden capabilities.

item.title: Learning Options for Compositional Motor Control with Adapter Banks
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Sreejan Kumar, Marcelo Mattar, Lea Duncker
arXiv:2609.17042v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning flexible motor primitives is a hallmark of skilled motor control. Recent neuroscience theory proposes that motor primitives may be implemented as low-rank perturbations of a shared recurrent network, but leaves open how such a system is learned. We translate this principle into a novel architecture for learning motor skills end-to-end: a shared recurrent core modulated by a bank of residual adapters, each selected by a discrete latent code. Trained on closed-loop biomechanical control, the adapters develop emergent low-rank perturbations of the recurrent dynamics despite no architectural rank constraint, placing task representations in disparate subspaces of the shared core network. A simple high-level policy over the learned options, optimized while the whole network is frozen, sequences the low-rank adapters to produce novel out-of-distribution movements. We demonstrate the ability to generalize to novel motor sequences within the closed-loop control setting, improving on the generalization error of a task-input-conditioned multitask baseline by approximately sevenfold.

item.title: Causal pieces: analysing and improving spiking neural networks piece by piece
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Dominik Dold, Philipp Christian Petersen
arXiv:2504.14015v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce "causal pieces", a novel concept for analysing spiking neural networks (SNNs), inspired by "linear pieces" used to study expressivity and trainability in artificial neural networks (ANNs). Causal pieces partition the input and parameter space of a feedforward SNN with single-spike coding into distinct regions where the same subnetwork causes the output spikes. For networks of current-based leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with large membrane time constants, we show that within each causal piece, output spike times are locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to inputs and network parameters. We further prove a lower bound on the approximation error that depends on the number of causal pieces. Thus, the number of causal pieces is a measure of the approximation capabilities of SNNs, which is valid despite spike-time discontinuities and applies to networks with both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Empirically, we find that parameter initialisations yielding more causal pieces on the training set strongly correlate with SNN training success across multiple benchmarks, including Yin-Yang, Fashion-MNIST, and EuroSAT. Moreover, simulations with standard single-spike LIF neurons indicate that our findings extend beyond the theoretically analysed regime. These results establish causal pieces as a powerful and principled tool for analysing and improving the computational capabilities of SNNs.

item.title: Judgment of Learning Reactivity for Extrinsic Cues - Experiment 3
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: SocArXiv
Zachary Adolph Niese et al.
Judgments of learning (JOLs) are a common measure in metamemory research, operationalized as an explicit judgment of the probability of recalling a word in a subsequent memory test. Previous work found the JOL measure to be reactive. That is, the mere act of providing JOLs alters memory performance dependent on the intrinsic cue of word pair type. Specifically, people exhibit better memory for related vs. unrelated word pairs, and the act of providing JOLs (vs. control) tends to strengthen the impact of this intrinsic cue. In two previous studies, we tested JOL reactivity based on extrinsic cues in which we manipulated reward value for word pairs. Participants exhibited better memory for high value pairs (worth 95 points) than for low value pairs (worth 5 points). There was also JOL reactivity, however, the effect of the extrinsic cue was weaker when participants gave JOLs (vs. control), even though the trial-level JOLs themselves were sensitive to a pair’s assigned point value. The two previous studies demonstrating this effect each relied on pure word lists consisting entirely of unrelated or weakly related word pairs. However, typical JOL studies employ mixed lists of related vs. unrelated word pairs. Thus, the current experiment tests if the JOL effect for the extrinsic cue reward replicates for a mixed list of unrelated and related word pairs. Additionally, we test whether the canonical JOL reactivity effect for the intrinsic cue relatedness is replicated in the presence of the salient extrinsic cue.

item.title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv AI
Xinyu Cao, Tianjie Ju, Zhuosheng Zhang
arXiv:2611.28574v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.

item.title: Seeking the Unfamiliar but Memorable: Conceptual Creativity as Meta-Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Mengye Ren
arXiv:2605.16477v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: What does it mean to create a new concept, rather than retrieve a familiar one? Repeatedly sampling a generative model at the same prompt produces variations with similar styles and typical content. We propose that creativity is the production of stimuli that are unfamiliar to an adaptive observer at first sight, but quickly learnable from a few exposures. We formalize this as a Creator-Appraiser pair: a Creator generates a candidate, an Appraiser adapts to it for a few inner-loop learning steps, and the Appraiser's improvement becomes the reward the Creator optimizes through. We instantiate the framework with diffusion as the Creator, an autoencoder Appraiser on MNIST, and a CLIP Appraiser with a low-rank adapter for natural images. With a frozen diffusion model and no additional language conditioning, the meta-learning gradient is enough to produce both stylistic variations and concept compositions beyond what the base model can generate on its own.

item.title: Social Bias Neurons in Multilingual Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Lance Calvin Lim Gamboa, Yue Feng, Mark Lee
arXiv:2611.32685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilingual models exhibit social bias when processing inputs pertaining to societal stereotypes. We adapt emerging mechanistic interpretability methods to pinpoint and characterize model components that encode this bias. We conduct our analysis across three instruction-tuned models, four languages, and seven bias dimensions. Specifically, we leverage multilingual bias benchmarks in implementing two methods for identifying social bias neurons: activation probability entropy and integrated gap gradients. We find the latter method to be more effective, as the neurons it isolates (which are largely concentrated at the model's deepest layers) lead to sharper decreases in model bias when suppressed. Further analysis reveals neuron distribution patterns differ between high- and low-resourced languages, suggesting that a language's representation in pretraining data influences how its biases are represented within model internals. Our results also indicate that neurons linked to gender, nationality, and social class biases overlap the most with neurons related to other bias dimensions, pointing to the pivotal role these three dimensions play in how models learn and handle bias.

item.title: Judgment of Learning Reactivity for Extrinsic Cues - Experiment 1
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: SocArXiv
Zachary Adolph Niese et al.
Research question: Do JOLs alter memory performance by strengthening extrinsic cues? In our experiment, participants will study 60 moderately-related word pairs that are presented in random order for a period of eight seconds. In one experimental condition, after the initial four seconds of word pair presentation, the JOL measure is displayed below for the subsequent four seconds. Participants are asked to estimate the probability of remembering the word pair in a subsequent memory test and indicate their JOL on a 0% –100% scale by positioning a bar along a continuous horizontal scale between 0 and 100. Additionally, a potential reward for each word pair given the participants remember it in the cued-recall test will be displayed. A point value is centered at the top of the screen above the word pairs for the full eight seconds of word pair presentation. Half of the words will randomly be assigned a low point value (5 points) and half of the words will be assigned a high point value (95 points). During learning, we will present the word pairs in different color fonts across conditions (blue vs. orange, value counterbalanced across participants) to ensure the difference in point value mains salient over the duration of the task. Following a distractor task, a cued recall test will be conducted. Baseline words of the word pairs will be presented one at a time in a random order, and participants will be required to type in the corresponding target words at their own pace.

item.title: Emergent Language as an Approach to Conscious AI
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Zengqing Wu, Chuan Xiao
arXiv:2606.06380v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The question of whether artificial systems can be conscious remains open, in part because existing approaches either evaluate systems against theory-derived checklists (discriminative) or engineer consciousness-inspired modules directly (architectural); both leave open whether observed structures are artifacts of human language priors. We propose a generative methodology: emergent language (EL) in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where agents start from minimal (no language, no concept of self, minimal exposure to human text) and develop communication under task pressure alone, ensuring causal attributability to task demands ratherthan inherited human language priors. We position our methodology by discussing how EL serves as a generative tool for studying consciousness-relevant structure, including the role of environment complexity and the interpretation of emergent communication. As a proof of concept, we instantiate this methodology in a minimal environment and show that agents develop self-referential communication, including an echo-mismatch detection circuit that is not predicted by task structure or architecture alone but emerges from a specific environmental affordance.

item.title: EEG-World: Context-Conditioned Dynamics of the Watching Brain
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Junxiang Zhang, Jiayu Zuo, Wenhao Ye, Junfeng Xia, Xiang Chen, Mo Wang, Quanying Liu
arXiv:2611.32825v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Brain encoding models predict neural responses from audiovisual input, but typically overlook how ongoing brain activity shapes an individual's response. We introduce EEG-World, a recurrent world model that forecasts 10 seconds of EEG band-power dynamics from 6 seconds of preceding EEG and the subsequent audiovisual stimulus. Pretrained on continuous EEG, EEG-World learns shared neural dynamics and adapts to unseen individuals through lightweight subject-specific readouts. Using 2,584 hours of EEG from 78 participants, we show that nonlinear recurrent forecasting surpasses strong history-aware linear baselines at scale. EEG-World achieves a forecasting correlation of 0.261 versus 0.233 for the strongest history-and-video linear model, with a 3.3-second forecasting-horizon advantage. Its learned dynamics transfer to unseen participants, outperforming the linear baseline in 23 of 24 individuals after calibration. While ongoing EEG history accounts for most predictive performance, controlled stimulus analyses reveal an additional video-dependent component. This component also enables evaluation of visual representations, with V-JEPA 2 improving clip-locked prediction by 35% over combined CLIP and DINOv2 features. Our results demonstrate the value of transferable neural dynamics for individual EEG forecasting and highlight the importance of separating state-driven from stimulus-driven predictability.

item.title: Mapping the invisible: Incidental spatial encoding through haptic exploration
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Vlachou, M. E., Kasim, S., mouchnino, L., Blouin, J.
Active touch provides rich spatial information about object shape. Whether this haptic information can be retained without an explicit memorisation goal remains unclear. Participants explored an unfamiliar two-dimensional raised-dot contour under different sensory conditions and memorisation instructions. Two haptic groups traced the contour hidden from view, either without advance knowledge of the memory tasks (Haptic-Naive) or with explicit memorisation instructions (Haptic-Informed). Reference groups traced the visible contour (Visuo-Haptic-Naive) or viewed it without tracing (Visual-Naive), both without memorisation instructions. Retention was assessed through manual shape reproduction and visual recognition, with a Random-Control group drawing arbitrary shapes as a reproduction baseline. Reproductions in all exploration groups were more similar to the target than arbitrary drawings, supporting incidental spatial encoding in the Haptic-Naive group. Memorisation instructions produced no detectable reproduction advantage but altered exploratory behaviour. Visual feedback improved online tracing without a detectable reproduction advantage over haptic-only exploration. Visual-Naive participants reproduced the shape more accurately than Haptic-Naive participants. Recognition scores were higher following memorisation instructions or exploration with visual information, although Haptic-Naive participants selected alternatives relatively similar to the target. Source-space EEG analyses in the Haptic-Naive group revealed widespread beta-power reductions across bilateral somatosensory, parietal, and occipital regions. Greater reductions in the left lateral occipital complex were associated with more accurate subsequent reproduction. Together, these findings indicate that active touch can support incidental spatial encoding and is associated with changes in cortical activity. The accessibility and use of the retained information are shaped by the goals and sensory context of exploration.

item.title: CoRe: Jointly Learning Contextual Representations for Understanding and Generation
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Hangke Sui, Chang Li, Yuyan Li, Mohammad Haris Baig, Daniel Ulbricht
arXiv:2611.31397v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce CoRe, in which understanding and generation jointly shape one contextual representation for images and one for text, trained from scratch. Each representation is read for understanding, conditions the other modality, and is the space in which that modality is generated by a continuous flow from Gaussian noise. With 383M parameters trained on CC12M and no pretrained language model, text encoder, or VAE at inference, CoRe matches a same-data contrastive-only baseline in global understanding and reaches COCO-30K FID 10.10, comparable to much larger generators built on pretrained components. In controlled comparisons at equal data and architecture, CoRe generates better in both directions (text to image and image to text) than a representation shaped by understanding alone and then frozen, and follows prompts better than generating in a space that understanding does not shape. In the other direction, with an attentive segmentation probe, on monocular depth, and when read by a frozen language model, CoRe surpasses the contrastive-only baseline: generation adds information that stronger readouts reach. Because generation runs inside the understanding representation, frozen real-image probes read and steer intermediate states and the model ranks its own samples without extra training. Because both modalities use continuous flows, both also distill to a few steps. Our controls indicate why one representation suffices: understanding organizes the representation semantically, while generation makes it retain more information.

item.title: Benchmarking machine learning across development reveals stage-specific neuroanatomical sex signatures.
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Poon, E., Honari, H., Ansarifar, J., Hong, D. S.
Machine learning (ML) offers powerful approaches for identifying multivariate patterns in neuroimaging data, yet the biological validity and interpretability of the discriminative patterns learned by such models remain incompletely understood. Here, we benchmarked multiple ML approaches for sex classification across development (8-21 years) on structural neuroimaging data and investigated the effects of age on model performance and feature stability. Linear and nonlinear models demonstrated comparable classification performance, indicating that high predictive accuracy can be achieved without relying on highly complex architectures; however, age-stratified analyses and cross-age generalization tests demonstrated that developmental stage influences classification performance, and consistency of learned neuroanatomical features. To assess biological interpretability, we applied SHAP and LIME explainability methods and developed a comprehensive framework for translating feature attributions into biologically interpretable patterns. Sex-discriminative regions were distributed across multiple cortical and subcortical structures and exhibited marked developmental variation. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of interpretable ML for developmental neuroimaging and highlight the importance of evaluating predictive performance while simultaneously taking biological validity, developmental specificity, and attribution stability into consideration.
